executiveSummary: GM0340's official identity, 2025 boundary, two BAG places, six BRT settlement labels, thirty neighbourhoods and headline CBS controls are coherent, and the deterministic ten-preset, six-checkpoint, eight-service contract passes. Release is nevertheless correction-required. The generic major-river screen gives Rhenen an exact 1.804674 m depth, 11,647 affected residents and fixed critical service consequences from T+24 through T+72 without selecting a Nederrijn level, Grebbedijk defence or breach state, connected footprint, probability, arrival, recession or dewatering case. This false precision is especially material where high Grebbeberg/Heuvelrug ground, low Binnenveld, the two normally inundating uiterwaarden and protected areas require different mechanisms. A common hash then ranks Elst West first and Heuvelrug Rhenen second across unrelated flood, wind, heat, winter, cyber, fire and compound maps; an explicit T+24 ignition at the official Grebbeberg neighbourhood centre still ranks its source neighbourhood only 16th of 30. Municipal evidence instead documents 46-74 mm/hour rain impacts on roads and buildings, hillslope infiltration and runoff, local groundwater pressure, distinct heat patterns, a heavily visited and inhabited nature-fire setting, roughly one million annual zoo visitors and congestion. Four static road-border records are only two through-corridors, N225 and N233; the congested Rijnbrug, river ferries, rail terminus, external acute care and all live route states remain unresolved. Forty-three registered water assets, provider territories, one grid-planning sample, antennas, schools and current Waterinfo/NDW/KNMI/RIVM snapshots provide context, not connected lifeline topology, live operation, outage, occupancy, backup or restoration. Exact local consequences and recovery must fail closed as Unknown/NoData until governed event, network, moving-population and first-72-hour action evidence is bound.

evidenceSources.publisher: Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek / PDOK / Kadaster
evidenceSources.title: E01 — GM0340 official 2025 municipality, neighbourhood, BAG place, BRT settlement and safety-region records
evidenceSources.edition: CBS Wijken en buurten 2025; generated source snapshots retrieved 31 August–3 September 2026
supports: Official and generated joins identify GM0340 as Rhenen in Utrecht and Veiligheidsregio Utrecht. Feature id and bundle code/name agree, and the generated centre [5.552548010686489, 51.97858438451181] lies inside the generalized 2025 boundary.

CBS reports 20,392 residents, density 485/km², 22.9% aged 65 or older and 2,746 one-person households. Thirty published neighbourhood rows total 20,395 residents, three higher (+0.015%) through source rounding; deterministic allocation reconciles model arithmetic without rewriting the observations.

The neighbourhood rows total 8,565 households and 4,665 rounded age-65-plus residents. District-heating share and public charging are null in all thirty rows; several dwelling and benefit fields cover 25 or 27 rows. Null, suppression and non-applicability remain NoData rather than zero.

BAG supplies two active places, Rhenen and Elst Ut. BRT supplies Rhenen, Elst and Achterberg as woonkernen, Heimerstein and Veeneind as gehuchten, and Laareind as a buurtschap. BAG, BRT and CBS features are distinct classes, not duplicate population measures.

The annual resident baseline does not measure incident-time zoo and nature visitors, overnight guests, workers, pupils, rail/bus/road/ferry users, responders, shelter occupants or people temporarily needing assistance.

evidenceSources.title: E02 — Regionaal Risicoprofiel Veiligheidsregio Utrecht 2023
supports: VRU says a single Grebbedijk breach between Rhenen and Wageningen can have major regional impact and explicitly names Rhenen, Veenendaal, Renswoude and Amersfoort among affected municipalities; disruptive conditions can require large-scale evacuation.

The profile treats river flooding, extreme-rain water nuisance, drought/nature fire, storm, ice and prolonged extreme weather as different mechanisms. Water nuisance or prolonged weather can impair access, while wind and ice can damage power and exhaust response resources.
Electricity/gas, drinking water, ICT/telecom, finance and water management are vital processes; digital IT/OT disruption can cascade through critical infrastructure.
A regional risk profile establishes relevance and coordination needs, not a selected local event, current warning, breach state, inundation field, outage, completed evacuation or T+72 forecast.

evidenceSources.publisher: Waterschap Vallei en Veluwe / Grebbedijk project partners
evidenceSources.title: E03 — Current Grebbedijk safety, monitoring, response and delivery lifecycle
supports: The project describes the existing Grebbedijk as strong and safe now while not meeting the future statutory standard; future extreme water can challenge height, stability and piping resistance. Planned strengthening is not proof of current failure.

The dike is inspected twice yearly and daily when high water is expected. At the stated orange trigger the operator adds full surveillance, sandbags and well control; at red it prepares for failure and residents are evacuated. A response protocol is not evidence that a trigger is active or an action complete.

In 2026 the contractor is preparing the execution design; physical dike work is expected in 2027–2030. Future works, traffic mitigation intent and project readiness cannot calibrate a present service or recovery value.

The project partners are Rhenen, Wageningen, Gelderland province, Rijkswaterstaat, Staatsbosbeheer, HWBP and Waterschap Vallei en Veluwe, demonstrating a cross-region dependency that one municipality scalar cannot govern.

evidenceSources.publisher: Waterschap Vallei en Veluwe / Grebbedijk project partners
evidenceSources.title: E04 — Grebbedijk landscape plan: two water systems, elevation and groundwater mechanisms
evidenceSources.edition: Definitive project-decision landscape plan inspected 3 September 2026
supports: The Grebbedijk separates two nearly distinct systems: the managed Nederrijn with incidental high water and the Binnenveld/Gelderse Vallei system draining mainly toward the Randmeren.
The plan distinguishes sandy, drought-sensitive Grebbeberg and Wageningen ridges from low Binnenveld and uiterwaarden, with locally important seepage; river clay and silt retain water longer.

These terrain, defence and groundwater differences contradict municipality-wide depth and a common neighbourhood order. The plan remains design/context evidence, not an incident footprint or live hydraulic state.

evidenceSources.title: E05 — Trendverkenning Visie op Rhenen 2035: climate, water, mobility and visitor context
evidenceSources.edition: Municipal trend exploration published for Visie op Rhenen 2035; planning evidence, not current measurements
supports: The municipal report says extreme 46–74 mm/hour rainfall can materially affect buildings and roads across Rhenen. It identifies permeable Heuvelrug storage, runoff toward lower areas and possible groundwater nuisance from higher levels on the Veluwe flanks.

It treats heat, drought and fire as linked but distinct: built areas retain heat; drought lowers groundwater and raises nature-fire risk; extreme rain needs locally distributed retention and infiltration.

The report says Ouwehands Dierenpark attracted around one million visitors annually from 2017–2019 and that extreme busy days caused substantial traffic nuisance; Heuvelrug nature recreation, events and overnight tourism add further moving population.

Planning scenarios, historic counts and stress-test illustrations establish mechanisms and data candidates, not day-specific occupancy, a live rainfall field, groundwater condition, traffic flow or completed mitigation.

evidenceSources.title: E06 — Rhenen nature-fire risk and public preparedness
supports: The municipality labels the current nature-fire risk as high on the inspected page and says drought and climate change have increased the risk in Rhenen.

It describes the Rhenen part of the Utrechtse Heuvelrug as both heavily visited and inhabited, asks visitors to keep official parking and emergency access clear, and directs people to a public road if fire occurs.

A time-varying public risk phase supports situational awareness only; it is not an ignition, perimeter, spread field, smoke plume, suppression state, route closure or forecast through the simulator's T+72 clock.

evidenceSources.title: E07 — Rhenen first-72-hour crisis preparedness and not-yet-available emergency support points
evidenceSources.edition: Current municipal preparedness page inspected 3 September 2026
supports: Rhenen tells households to prepare water, shelf-stable food, light, power and cash for the first 72 hours and to assist less-mobile people, people with language barriers and isolated neighbours.

The municipality and VRU are developing a network of emergency support points, but the page says a nearby point will be published once one exists. It therefore does not establish a currently available location, staffing, stock, accessibility, capacity or activation.

The municipality prepares for nature fire, flooding, major digital disruption and prolonged power outage. Guidance and intended support are not observations of household preparedness or completed response actions.

evidenceSources.publisher: Provincie Utrecht / Rijkswaterstaat / ProRail / OVapi / ferry operators
evidenceSources.title: E08 — N233 Rijnbrug and deployed static multimodal transport context
evidenceSources.edition: Province page updated 26 June 2026; NWB-Light 1 August 2026; ProRail and GTFS snapshots retrieved August–September 2026
supports: NWB produces four border records: N225 connects Wageningen–Rhenen–Utrechtse Heuvelrug and N233 connects Veenendaal–Rhenen–Buren across the Rijnbrug. They are two physical through-corridors, not four independent parallel capacities; the model's nominal 150-unit values are scenario units.

The province reports recurring N233 congestion at the Rijnbrug, roughly 1,500 vehicles per hour per direction at busy times, and only an option study for later widening. This establishes a bottleneck context, not a closure, damage state, guaranteed capacity or completed upgrade.

The generated static context contains Rhenen station and 33 spatial GTFS stop areas, but rail terminates at Rhenen and does not cross the river. Static railway/timetable geometry proves neither service operation nor passenger, evacuation or repair capacity.

The road graph omits the Ingen–Elst vehicle ferry and seasonal Rhenen–Lienden passenger ferry. The operator page reported normal Ingen–Elst service when inspected, but schedules and a transient human-readable notice are not proof of scenario-time operation, load limit suitability, emergency priority or T+72 continuity.
NWB geometry is Mobility and assumed road-logistics Supply context only; it is never power, water, drainage, gas, telecom or facility topology.

evidenceSources.publisher: Het Waterschapshuis / Stichting Mijn Aansluiting / Netbeheer Nederland / RDI / DUO / RIVM / Rijkswaterstaat
evidenceSources.title: E09 — Public water, utility, communications, education, acute-care and current-context deployment for GM0340
evidenceSources.edition: Deployment snapshots retrieved 2–3 September 2026; centre-point provider WMS queried 3 September 2026
supports: Full non-generalized-boundary containment assigns 43 public water objects: 35 weirs, five surface-water pumps, two sewer pumps and RWZI Rhenen. Five records have non-null capacities. Register status 'gerealiseerd' does not prove connected catchment, current operation, power, control, reserve, backup or restoration.

The assets span Waterschap Vallei en Veluwe and HDSR responsibilities. HDSR's public chain says RWZI Rhenen treats Rhenen, Elst, Amerongen and Leersum and discharges to the Nederrijn; this cross-boundary role is absent from service causality.

Public Domain Mijn Aansluiting centre-point queries identify Stedin for electricity/gas, Vitens for drinking water and Ziggo for media; drainage returns no provider. Territory at one point is not municipal topology, service availability, pressure/quality, outage or repair state.

The single NBNL postcode sample 3911XN resolves to Stedin area TS059_10 Veenendaal 2 and reports queues and 28 planning projects with earliest project year 2030, while key existing/required MW values are null. It is neither municipal coverage nor live load, headroom, outage or restoration.

RDI assigns 34 sites and 75 antenna installations, including twenty mobile and seven fixed-link sites; DUO assigns ten education locations. These registers do not establish radio coverage/backhaul/power/backup or shelter occupancy, staffing, supplies and care capacity.

No RIVM acute-care point lies inside GM0340; the nearest questionnaire emergency department is Ziekenhuis Gelderse Vallei in Ede, 8.02 km straight-line from the municipal centre. The questionnaire says 24/7 and reports 16 treatment rooms and 22,000 2025 visits, but not live acceptance, staffing, occupancy, route or generator state.

No KNMI station/event, RIVM PM2.5 station, Waterinfo point or NDW situation is assigned inside GM0340 in the bounded snapshots. The named Waterinfo point Rhenen Grebbeberg lies on the opposite bank and is assigned to GM1740; its 2 September 17:30Z observation was 612 cm NAP and forecasts exist only through T+24 in the deployed match. Point/horizon absence is NoData, never zero hazard or an all-clear.

residualLimitations: This audits a deterministic first-72-hour exercise model, not a warning, forecast, hydraulic assessment, evacuation order, fire perimeter, outage statement, route guarantee or operator commitment.
CBS 2025 cells are rounded/suppressed and annual residents do not measure zoo/nature/event/overnight/worker/traveller populations; allocated totals are model arithmetic, not observations.

Generalized municipality/neighbourhood geometry and label points cannot resolve dike sections, hydraulic connectivity, hillslope flow, groundwater, sewer catchments, fuel continuity, buildings or exact route intersections.
The Grebbedijk is described as currently safe while needing strengthening to a future standard; project lifecycle and risk protocol do not establish a current breach, alert, action or completed work.
The project landscape and municipal climate documents are planning/stress-test context, not incident-time river, rainfall, groundwater, heat or recovery values.
The current municipal high nature-fire phase is time-varying situational context, not the canonical scenario time, ignition, plume, route closure or T+72 prediction.
